messages.author: ea7d65e6eb7bf605
messages.subject: Spatial and Temporal replication
parts:
I am working with a pretty standard point-count occupancy data set: I
have 232 sites that were surveyed between 1 and 5 times in one
season. (single-season, closed). These sites are then distributed
across 108 patches of habitat with 1 - 7(or so) sites per patch. Two
of my covariates are specific to the patch (patch area and patch
isolation), but then two of them are specific to the site/point (basal
area and grass cover). I have successfully fitted models using the
site as the experimental unit, but there are issues with independence
between sites for the patch-level covariates. I am wondering if there
is a way to set this up in an unmarked frame with a different
experimental unit for different covariates (like a split-plot
design).

My only thought so far is that each spatial/temporal replicate
combination is one actual replicate. So that say one patch had 3
sites within it, two of the sites were sampled 4 times, and the third
was sampled 3 times. then the experimental unit would be the patch
with 11 replicates, averaging the site-level covariates across those
11 replicates. This method is straightforward but some information is
lost. If there is a way to accommodate this split-plot type design
please let me know. Any advice would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Paul Taillie
North Carolina State University

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Spatial and Temporal replication
parts:
hi Paul and Matthew,

fitting patch ID as a covariate would not account correctly for the two patch-specific covariates, but probably is the most appropriate that you can do in unmarked. To fully accommodate the nested (split-plot) structure, you would have to conduct an analysis in BUGS.

Regards -- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: Spatial and Temporal replication
parts:
Hi Paul,

not directly, but the usual way how people deal with these split-plot designs in the age of random effects (= now) is to fit a set of random effects for the patch factor. That should do it.

Kind regards -- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Spatial and Temporal replication
parts:
Hey Paul,

A good reference for building multilevel models is Gelman and Hill (2007) - Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models.  They describe exactly what Marc speaks of, where random effects at some spatial level of a nested hierarchy are defined and allow you to model the effect of covariates that are specific to that level.  All of their model code is written in R and BUGS.


http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/arm/
